Now I have a complete picture. Here's the concrete architecture.

---

## Architecture recommendation

### 1. The single best architecture

**A single static HTML page, generated by a short Python build script that reads your existing `bibliographie_air_interieur.bib` and `syntheses_bibliographie_air_interieur.md` and produces a `data.json` file. The page uses vanilla JS (no framework) to render, filter, and navigate the entries. PDFs are served directly from the site.**

Why this and not something else:
- **Not Quarto/Hugo/Jekyll**: you don't need a static site generator. You have one page of content. Adding a generator adds a dependency, a config surface, and a learning curve for nothing.
- **Not client-side parsing of the raw markdown**: your syntheses file is 237 KB. Parsing it in the browser every load is wasteful and fragile. A build script converts it once.
- **Not a multi-file framework (React, Vue, etc.)**: you have 60 entries, not 6000. Vanilla JS with `document.createElement` or template literals is all you need.
- **Python build script** because your group already uses Python (PSL/ENS), and `bibtexparser` handles your `.bib` file reliably. The script will be ~120 lines.

### 2. One page, not multiple pages

**One page.** The reasons are structural:

- You have ~60 bibliography entries. That's a long list, not a complex hierarchy. A multi-page site (one page per entry, or per chapter) creates a navigation problem worse than the one it solves.
- The note's argument is a single summary paragraph (the résumé from the title page). It doesn't need its own page.
- Filtering (by author, theme, type) works far better on a single page: the user sees results instantly, no page reload.
- `Ctrl+F` searches everything at once.

Layout: a top section with the note's argument and a link to download the compiled PDF, then a filter bar, then an accordion list of all entries (collapsed by default, expandable on click).

### 3. Data structure

The build script merges two sources into one `data.json`:

**From `bibliographie_air_interieur.bib`**, extract per entry:
- `key` (e.g. `Kingdon1984Agendas`)
- `author` (split into individual surnames for filtering)
- `title`
- `year`
- `type` (book, article, incollection, report, online)
- `url` (if present)
- `journal` / `booktitle` (for display)

**From `syntheses_bibliographie_air_interieur.md`**, split by the `## \`Key\`` headers and extract:
- `access_status` (`FULLTEXT`, `FULLTEXT-CIBLE`, `PARTIAL`, `INDIRECT`)
- `base_de_lecture` (the source description line)
- `body_html` (the full synthesis converted to HTML)
- `page_refs` (extracted page references like `pp. 3-4`, `pp. 18-20` — these become PDF page links)
- `in_main_bib` (boolean: true if in the main bib, false if marked `[hors bibliographie actuelle]`)

**Themes are assigned manually** in a small `themes.json` file (or a YAML block at the top of the build script). You have 4 natural thematic clusters from the note's structure:

| Theme tag | Corresponds to |
|---|---|
| `publicisation` | Ch. 2 — quantification, visibilité experte, mise à l'agenda |
| `imputation` | Ch. 3 — difficulté d'imputation, causes multiples, risque politique |
| `instruments` | Ch. 4 — étiquetage, guides, surveillance ERP, responsabilisation |
| `inegalites` | Ch. 5 — précarité énergétique, sélectivité sociale |
| `cadre-theorique` | Transversal — Kingdon, Gusfield, Lascoumes, Borraz, etc. |
| `source-institutionnelle` | Décrets, rapports, pages ministérielles, données |

Each bib key gets 1-3 theme tags. The build script reads these mappings and attaches them to the JSON entries.

**Output `data.json` structure** (one entry):
```json
{
  "key": "Kingdon1984Agendas",
  "author": ["Kingdon, John W."],
  "author_surnames": ["Kingdon"],
  "title": "Agendas, Alternatives, and Public Policies",
  "year": 1984,
  "type": "book",
  "url": null,
  "journal": null,
  "booktitle": null,
  "access_status": "FULLTEXT-CIBLE",
  "themes": ["publicisation", "cadre-theorique"],
  "in_main_bib": true,
  "pdf_file": null,
  "page_refs": [
    {"label": "pp. 3-4", "page": 3},
    {"label": "pp. 18-20", "page": 18}
  ],
  "synthesis_html": "<p>Kingdon reste l'un des points d'appui..."
}
```

### 4. Author / source / theme navigation

A **filter bar** at the top of the entry list, with three independent facets that combine with AND logic:

- **Author dropdown**: populated from `author_surnames` across all entries. Selecting "Le Bourhis" shows only entries where Le Bourhis is an author.
- **Theme tags**: a row of clickable pills (`publicisation`, `imputation`, `instruments`, `inegalites`, `cadre-theorique`, `source-institutionnelle`). Click to toggle. Active tags are highlighted.
- **Type filter**: pills for `book`, `article`, `incollection`, `report`, `online`.
- **Access status filter**: pills for `FULLTEXT`, `FULLTEXT-CIBLE`, `PARTIAL`, `INDIRECT`.
- **Text search**: a simple input field that filters entries by matching against title, author, key, and synthesis text.

Implementation: each entry card has `data-*` attributes. Filtering is just toggling `display: none` on cards that don't match. ~30 lines of JS.

### 5. PDF page links

Your syntheses already contain page references (e.g., "pp. 3-4", "pp. 18-20"). The build script extracts these with a regex like `pp?\.\s*(\d+)` and stores them as structured data.

On the site, each entry card shows clickable page links:

```html
<a href="papers/filename.pdf#page=18" target="_blank">pp. 18-20</a>
```

**The `#page=N` fragment** is supported by Chrome, Firefox, and Edge's built-in PDF viewers. It opens the PDF scrolled to that page. This is the standard mechanism; no special library is needed.

For entries where you have the PDF in `papers/`, the build script needs a mapping from bib key to PDF filename. This is a manual mapping (a small dict in the build config) because your PDF filenames don't match your bib keys:

```python
PDF_MAP = {
    "CrespinFerron2016ScandaleRecherchePublic": "crespin-2016-un-scandale-a-la-recherche-de-son-public.pdf",
    "HourcadeLeBourhis2024PolitiqueEtiquette": "hourcade-2024-la-politique-de-letiquette-....pdf",
    "LeBourhis2019AirInterieurResponsabilisation": "le-bourhis-2019-du-prive-au-public-....pdf",
    # etc.
}
```

For entries where you have a URL but no local PDF (like the ADEME guides, Légifrance decrees), the card links directly to the external URL.

### 6. Download links

Each card has two link types:

- **"Ouvrir" (open)**: `<a href="papers/file.pdf#page=N" target="_blank">` — opens inline in browser.
- **"Télécharger" (download)**: `<a href="papers/file.pdf" download>` — triggers browser download dialog.

For the compiled research note itself, a prominent button at the top of the page:

```html
<a href="note_recherche_collective_air_interieur.pdf" download class="btn">
  Télécharger la note de recherche (PDF)
</a>
```

### 7. Folder structure

```
travail_collectif/
├── site/                          ← deployed to GitHub Pages
│   ├── index.html                 ← the single page
│   ├── style.css                  ← styling (can be inlined)
│   ├── app.js                     ← filtering + accordion logic
│   ├── data.json                  ← generated by build script
│   ├── note.pdf                   ← copy of compiled note
│   └── papers/                    ← copies of source PDFs
│       ├── crespin-2016-un-scandale-....pdf
│       ├── hourcade-2024-la-politique-....pdf
│       └── ...
├── build_site.py                  ← build script (~120 lines)
├── themes.json                    ← manual theme assignments
├── bibliographie_air_interieur.bib        ← source (unchanged)
├── syntheses_bibliographie_air_interieur.md  ← source (unchanged)
├── note_recherche_collective_air_interieur.tex  ← source
├── note_recherche_collective_air_interieur.pdf  ← compiled
└── papers/                        ← original PDFs (unchanged)
```

GitHub Pages is configured to serve from `site/` (via GitHub Actions, since GitHub Pages can't serve from an arbitrary subfolder natively — you'd use a workflow that copies `site/` contents to the `gh-pages` branch, or you deploy the whole `site/` folder).

### 8. Phased implementation plan

**Phase 1 — Data pipeline (day 1)**
- Write `build_site.py`: parse bib, split syntheses markdown, merge, output `data.json`.
- Write `themes.json`: assign 1-3 theme tags to each of the ~60 entries. This is manual but takes 20 minutes with the note open beside it.
- Write `PDF_MAP` in the build script: map bib keys → PDF filenames for the 8 PDFs you have locally.
- Validate: run the script, inspect `data.json`.

**Phase 2 — Core page (day 1-2)**
- Write `index.html`: the note's résumé at top, download button, filter bar, empty container for cards.
- Write `app.js`: fetch `data.json`, render cards (collapsed), implement accordion expand/collapse.
- Write `style.css`: minimal styling. Cards with border, status badges with color, responsive layout.
- Test locally (just open `index.html` in a browser).

**Phase 3 — Navigation + PDF links (day 2)**
- Add filter logic (author dropdown, theme pills, text search).
- Add PDF open/download links per entry.
- Add page-specific links for entries that have `page_refs`.
- Test PDF `#page=N` links in Chrome/Firefox.

**Phase 4 — Deploy (day 2-3)**
- Copy PDFs and note.pdf into `site/papers/` and `site/`.
- Add a GitHub Actions workflow (`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`) that runs `build_site.py` and deploys `site/` to GitHub Pages.
- Or simpler: just commit the generated `site/` folder and configure GitHub Pages to serve from it.
- Test the live URL.

### 9. Hidden pitfalls

1. **PDF filenames with spaces and accents.** Your `papers/` folder has filenames like `"Ferron_Hourcade_Lebourhis_2018 Comment s'approprier un probleme final.pdf"`. These must be URL-encoded in links (`%20` for spaces). The build script should handle this. Better yet: rename the PDFs to slug-based names (`ferron-hourcade-lebourhis-2018.pdf`) when copying them to `site/papers/`.

2. **GitHub Pages file size limits.** GitHub Pages has a soft limit of 1 GB for the site and individual files should stay under 100 MB. Your largest PDF is 8.7 MB (`Etat-de-lart-Qualite-de-lair-interieur-Vdef-30-10.pdf`). You're fine, but don't add many more large PDFs without checking.

3. **`#page=N` doesn't work on mobile.** Mobile browsers (iOS Safari, Android Chrome) typically download PDFs or open them in a separate viewer app that ignores the `#page=` fragment. This is a browser limitation, not something you can fix. Add the page number in the visible link text so mobile users can navigate manually.

4. **The syntheses markdown uses backtick-quoted BibTeX keys in headers** (`## \`Key\``). Your regex parser must handle the backticks. A naïve split on `## ` would also match subheadings within entries. Split on `^## \`` (line start + ## + backtick) to be safe.

5. **Some syntheses entries are marked `[hors bibliographie actuelle]`** and don't have a matching bib entry. The build script must handle entries present in one source but not the other: a bib entry without a synthesis gets a "pas encore de fiche" placeholder; a synthesis without a bib entry gets its citation built from the synthesis header.

6. **The bib file has `@report` entries.** Standard BibTeX doesn't define `@report`; `bibtexparser` in Python handles it fine, but double-check that it parses correctly. If not, treat them as `@techreport` or `@misc`.

7. **Private repo + public Pages URL.** Your classmates can see the site, but so can anyone with the URL. That's fine per your stated decision, but be aware that search engines will eventually index it unless you add a `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` tag.

### 10. The one UX pattern that matters

**The "annotated bibliography as interface."**

The killer feature of this site is not the technology — it's the synthesis file you already wrote. You have 60 entries, each with a structured reading note, an access status, page references, and mobilization guidance. Most student bibliographies are flat lists of citations. Yours is an actual research tool.

The UX pattern that makes this sing: **every entry is a compact card showing citation + status badge + PDF button. Click the card, the full synthesis unfolds. Page references inside the synthesis are clickable and open the PDF at the right page.**

This means a classmate can:
1. Filter to "instruments" theme → see the 10 entries relevant to Chapter 4
2. Spot that Hourcade & Le Bourhis 2024 is `[FULLTEXT]` → confidence that the synthesis is solid
3. Click the card → read the full synthesis including what can be mobilized and what cannot
4. Click "pp. 117-136" → the PDF opens at the right page in the browser
5. Click "Télécharger" → save the PDF locally

This is the pattern. It turns a static bibliography into a navigable, filterable, PDF-linked research workspace. No academic group project site I've seen does this well, and you already have all the content to make it work.
